title: Short Stuff: Petrichor
summary: Josh and Chuck explain petrichor, the earthy smell after rain. They cover its name, coined in the 1960s by Isabel Joy Bear and Richard Thomas in the journal Nature; the three contributing sources: geosmin from soil bacteria (Streptomyces), ozone from lightning, and plant terpenes; how raindrops aerosolize these compounds (MIT research in 2015 using high-speed cameras); why light rain smells stronger and why wind carries the scent; why humans are highly sensitive to geosmin compared with sharks and blood; geosmin in beets, wine and mineral water; geosmin use in Indian attar and perfume; and why city rain smells cleaner than country rain.
topics: why rain smells cleaner in the city

segments.title: Opening banter and naming petrichor
segments.summary: Josh opens the short by noting the good smell after rain and introduces the term petrichor. They discuss its origin: coined in Australia in the 1960s by Isabel Joy Bear and Richard Thomas in an article in Nature, from Greek words for stone and the fluid in the veins of the gods. They say the smell comes from a combination of three sources.

segments.title: Geosmin from soil bacteria and aerosolization
segments.summary: The first ingredient is geosmin, made by Streptomyces bacteria when they die and are consumed by other bacteria. Bear and Thomas identified it in the 1960s, but how it reached the air was unclear until MIT researchers in 2015 used high-speed cameras to show raindrops trap air bubbles that burst and aerosolize the compound. Light rain smells stronger because wind can spread the aerosol.

segments.title: Human sensitivity to geosmin vs sharks
segments.summary: Humans are far more sensitive to geosmin than most animals, detecting it at about five parts per trillion, which is more sensitive than sharks are to blood (about one part per billion, though the shark claim is partly overstated). The hosts say the evolutionary reason is unclear, possibly related to finding water. Geosmin also appears in beets, wine and mineral water.

segments.title: Geosmin in perfume
segments.summary: The hosts note that geosmin was captured and sold in India as mettica atar, and that it is becoming a perfume ingredient in the United States and Europe.

segments.title: Ozone from lightning and city vs country rain
segments.summary: The second ingredient is ozone, formed when lightning splits oxygen molecules and combines them into O3. Rain in the city smells cleaner than in the country because there is less soil and so less geosmin, letting the crisp ozone smell stand out more.
topics: why rain smells cleaner in the city

segments.title: Terpenes from plants
segments.summary: The third ingredient is terpenes, the compounds that give plants their smells. They are thought to be activated during rainstorms, and heavy rain can break off dry plant material and release them, similar to crushing dried herbs. Like geosmin, they are aerosolized by raindrops.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck close the short, suggesting listeners can use the term petrichor, and note the show is produced by iHeartRadio's HowStuffWorks.
